children.text: A property manager opens the monthly utility file and finds three problems at once. The building's bulk electricity bill is higher than the operating budget, a water leak has gone unnoticed, and residents are challenging charges based on estimates they don't understand. The manager can spend days comparing invoices, reviewing spreadsheets, and explaining allocation formulas, yet still lack the unit-level evidence needed to settle disputes confidently.

That's the operating gap total meter services are designed to close. Instead of treating metering, billing, maintenance, compliance, and tenant support as separate responsibilities, a turnkey provider connects them under one managed program. The owner gets clearer consumption data and a defined recovery process, while residents receive bills tied to measured use rather than an opaque building-wide average.

For multi-family, condominium, mixed-use, student housing, and commercial properties, the strongest model goes further than equipment installation. A provider owns and maintains the metering infrastructure over a long-term agreement, manages the billing workflow, coordinates regulatory requirements, and supports the property after launch. That structure can reduce the owner's administrative load without requiring an upfront equipment purchase.

The recommendation is straightforward. Don't buy meters first and figure out service later. Define the desired billing model, compliance responsibilities, resident communications, maintenance obligations, and exit terms before approving a project. In Ontario, the regulatory framework makes that discipline especially important because unit sub-metering is a licensed commercial activity governed by consumer-facing rules.

Understanding the Key Concepts

Total meter services means more than installing a device beside each electrical panel. It's a coordinated operating model that measures utility use, converts readings into charges, supports collections, maintains equipment, and keeps the program aligned with applicable rules.

Think of a building's bulk meter as a shared water supply. It tells you how much water enters the property, but it doesn't show which apartment used what. Individual submeters act like separate faucets with their own readings. The provider can then associate consumption with a specific suite, commercial unit, common area, or building system.

The same logic can apply to several utility categories:

  • Electricity submetering: Tracks unit-level electricity consumption and separates tenant loads from common-area use.
  • Water submetering: Measures suite and shared-area consumption, with leak and flood detection supporting faster incident response.
  • Gas allocation: Assigns unit-level gas consumption where the jurisdiction and building design permit it.
  • Thermal metering: Measures heating or cooling energy in properties with shared thermal systems.
  • Common-area metering: Separates elevators, corridors, mechanical systems, parking areas, and other shared loads from private consumption.

Why measured usage matters

Bulk billing forces an owner to choose an allocation method. That method might use suite size, occupancy assumptions, historical averages, or another formula. Those approaches can be administratively convenient, but they don't show actual consumption inside each unit.

Unit-level data supports itemized billing and gives residents a clearer explanation for their charges. It also gives owners a way to identify unusual patterns, investigate suspected leaks, and compare common-area demand with tenant demand. The value isn't limited to invoice accuracy. Visibility can change behaviour because residents can connect everyday consumption with their own costs.

Ontario's framework treats this work as a regulated activity. Under O. Reg. 443/07, Ontario established a formal licensing regime in 2007 for the commercial offering or provision of smart meters, metering equipment, and associated unit sub-metering services. The regulation requires providers to obtain and maintain a licence, with a non-refundable $1,000 application fee for a new licence and an $800 annual registration fee under the Ontario Energy Board's rules (Ontario's regulation governing unit sub-metering).

The provider-owned model

In a provider-owned arrangement, the service company supplies, installs, commissions, monitors, and replaces the equipment under a long-term agreement. The owner avoids turning metering hardware into a separate capital project and instead evaluates the program as an operating service.

That distinction matters for smaller buildings as well as large portfolios. The right question isn't whether a property can install meters. It's whether the owner can operate accurate billing, maintain the equipment, answer resident questions, manage collections, and meet regulatory duties without creating a new internal department.

Equipment selection and site design

The provider should start with a site assessment, not a catalogue. Engineers and electricians need to understand electrical distribution, plumbing layouts, mechanical systems, communications pathways, suite access, common-area loads, and local approval requirements.

A suitable design should identify:

  • Meter location: The installation point must support safe access, reliable readings, and practical maintenance.
  • Utility scope: The design should distinguish private loads, shared loads, and any services that can't be allocated at unit level.
  • Data requirements: The provider should define reading frequency, data retention, exception reporting, and billing integration before hardware arrives.
  • Regulatory fit: Equipment and installation practices must match the applicable Canadian or U.S. requirements. For electricity programs in Canada, Measurement Canada considerations should be addressed during design rather than after installation.
  • Risk monitoring: Water programs should include leak and flood detection where the building's risk profile justifies it.

Installation and commissioning

Installation is more than fastening meters in place. The project team must label devices, verify wiring or piping, confirm unit associations, test communications, and document the relationship between each meter and the correct service address.

Commissioning should include controlled tests and a sign-off process. A provider that can't show how it verified meter-to-suite mapping creates a future billing problem. The owner should receive an asset register, commissioning records, escalation contacts, and a clear process for correcting data exceptions.

The resident experience needs a named support path. A help desk, online payment process, account history, move-out reconciliation, and documented dispute escalation can prevent the property manager from becoming the default utility call centre.

Ongoing service should cover routine monitoring, troubleshooting, meter replacements, communications failures, and billing exceptions. Owners should also receive reports that separate consumption, recoveries, unresolved accounts, vacant units, common-area loads, and abnormal readings.

Terms that deserve negotiation

Your service-level agreement should define response priorities, escalation contacts, meter replacement procedures, data availability, billing correction timelines, planned maintenance, and resident communications. Avoid vague language such as “commercially reasonable support” unless the contract also explains what happens when support fails.

Ask for clear answers on:

  • Availability: What system functions must remain operational, and how will interruptions be reported?
  • Accuracy: What testing, validation, and correction process applies to questionable readings?

  • Data access: Can the owner export consumption and billing records if management changes?
  • Termination: What happens to equipment, resident accounts, open balances, and data at expiry?
  • Rate changes: Which charges can change, how much notice is required, and who approves the change?
  • Compliance: Which party tracks regulatory amendments and updates Conditions of Service?

Compliance and Project Management

Compliance failures rarely begin with a defective meter. They usually begin with an unclear responsibility matrix, an incomplete site design, a missed approval, or a resident notice that wasn't coordinated with the billing launch.

Ontario operators need to treat licensing and consumer protection as core project work. The Ontario Energy Board's Unit Sub-Metering Code defines unit sub-metering as the provision and maintenance of unit sub-meters in multi-unit complexes, including billing and collection. It also requires billing calculations to be grounded in measured usage, with estimation used only when relevant usage data has been unavailable for 12 consecutive months within the prior two years (Ontario's Unit Sub-Metering Code).

A practical compliance checklist

  1. Confirm the jurisdiction. Identify the province, state, utility territory, building classification, and services included in the program.
  2. Verify provider authority. In Ontario, confirm that the electricity unit sub-meter provider is licensed and prepared to follow the OEB code.
  3. Map the loads. Document each private and common-area load before selecting equipment or building the billing model.
  4. Review approvals. Assign responsibility for electrical permits, plumbing approvals, inspections, equipment certifications, and utility coordination.
  5. Validate the design. Have qualified professionals review capacity, safety, communications, and meter placement. Teams working in U.S. jurisdictions can use a resource on NEC compliant load calculations as part of their electrical planning process.
  6. Build the resident workflow. Prepare notices, account setup, move-in instructions, payment channels, dispute handling, and accessibility support.
  7. Test before billing. Verify meter identity, readings, data transmission, rate logic, invoice formatting, and exception handling.
  8. Create an audit file. Store permits, approvals, commissioning records, customer agreements, notices, billing rules, and service logs in one controlled location.

Assign ownership by phase

The property owner approves the commercial model and ensures the project supports lease, condominium, financing, and asset-management requirements. The property manager coordinates access, resident communications, vacant suites, and site operations.

Engineering teams define the technical design and load allocation. Electricians and other trades perform the physical work under the approved design. The metering provider should coordinate procurement, installation planning, commissioning, billing configuration, maintenance, and regulatory documentation.

In August 2025, OEB code amendments introduced updated consumer-protection requirements for Ontario unit sub-meter customers, including clear winter disconnection policies, twice-yearly consumer-protection notices, and revised Conditions of Service (OEB unit sub-metering rules and code updates). Treat those requirements as an operating workflow, not a legal footnote. Payment disputes, arrears, notices, reconnection, and winter restrictions must be reflected in the billing system and staff procedures.

Practical rule: Don't schedule go-live until the technical file and the resident communications file are both complete.

Week 7

The provider integrates the metering system with billing and account-management processes. Testing should verify device identity, reading transmission, unit assignment, common-area separation, invoice logic, and exception reporting.

The owner's team should review sample invoices and confirm that resident names, suite identifiers, notices, payment instructions, and dispute contacts are correct.

Week 8

Commissioning and training take place. The provider activates the system, delivers documentation, and trains property staff on dashboards, exceptions, resident questions, and escalation procedures.

Weeks 9 and 10

The program enters go-live and post-launch support. The provider monitors the first billing cycle, resolves data exceptions, supports residents, and reports early operational issues. The owner should schedule a formal review after launch to confirm that service levels, communications, and recovery processes match the agreement.

Commercial Considerations for Property Owners

A building can lower its exposure to utility costs while giving residents a clearer connection between consumption and payment. That business case has two parts: cost recovery, through unit-level billing tied to measured use, and demand management, through visibility that can reveal waste and encourage conservation.

Ontario billing evidence provides a useful reference point. An independent comparison found that approximately 170,000 customers averaged $66.52 per month under sub-metering, compared with $78.43 under individual metering by the local distribution company. The difference was $11.91 per month. The analysis also estimated that 94% of customers paid less with sub-metering than they would have with LDC metering, while 6% paid more (Ontario sub-metering bill comparison).

Those results do not predict the return for every property. Rates, service charges, allocation rules, building design, vacancy, resident consumption, financing terms, and provider fees can change the outcome. Owners should therefore test building-specific billing scenarios rather than assume that bulk billing is automatically simpler or cheaper.

Consumption changes are part of the value

A Navigant study based on Ontario apartment and condominium data reported an average first-year reduction of 139 kWh per unit per month, described as a 40% decrease, after sub-metering. It projected approximately 9.4 billion kWh in electricity savings over 20 years if the approach were implemented across eligible units (Navigant's Ontario sub-metering analysis).

That finding broadens the investment case. The owner is not only recovering part of the utility bill. Residents can see their usage, adjust behaviour, and contribute to lower aggregate demand. The result may support operating-cost control and reduce reliance on blunt bulk averages.

A separate Ontario analysis estimated $1.2 billion in avoided electricity-system costs over 20 years if eligible multi-residential buildings adopted sub-metering (Building Energy Innovators Council analysis of broad-based sub-metering benefits). Treat that estimate as system-level context, not as a guaranteed property return. It shows why measured consumption can matter beyond monthly invoice recovery.

Portfolio-specific decision making

Small portfolios need a disciplined scope. A smaller building may still gain from leak detection, clearer unit allocation, and outsourced resident support. Request a building-specific model covering installation constraints, account volumes, common-area treatment, service charges, and the long-term contract. Scale alone does not determine viability.

Condominium corporations need governance clarity. Directors should confirm who owns the equipment, who approves billing rules, how resident disputes are handled, and whether the program fits the declaration documents and operating practices. Clear communication matters because a technically correct invoice can still create conflict when residents do not understand the change.

Mixed-use properties need load separation. Retail, office, residential, parking, mechanical systems, and shared amenities can operate on different schedules and consume power differently. Treating the property as one residential block can create weak allocation logic and difficult reconciliation.

Student and affordable housing requires accessible support. Residents may have different payment patterns, move frequently, or need clearer explanations of charges. Require plain-language notices, accessible account support, and procedures for move-ins, move-outs, arrears, and disputes. Site staff should not carry the entire administrative burden.

Model the full return

A credible business case should cover:

  • Recovery potential: Estimate which utility costs can be assigned to units under applicable rules and agreements.
  • Provider charges: Separate metering, billing, maintenance, account, payment, and resident-support costs.
  • Capital treatment: Compare the 20-year provider-owned model with owner-financed procurement and future replacement obligations.
  • Operational savings: Estimate staff time saved through outsourced readings, invoicing, collections support, and issue resolution.
  • Risk reduction: Include leak alerts, clearer dispute evidence, documented compliance, and less manual allocation.
  • Tenant impact: Test proposed charges against different resident profiles instead of relying on one average.
  • Exit exposure: Review termination fees, equipment transfer, data access, and transition support before approval.

The Ontario operating base shows that sub-metering has established processes rather than being a niche service. Licensed unit sub-meter providers served 352,792 residential and small-business units in 2021–2022, with reported electricity conservation of 588,475,056 kWh per year. Use that scale as evidence of market maturity, not as a substitute for property-level diligence.

The 20-year provider-owned model deserves specific scrutiny. It can preserve owner capital and place long-term equipment responsibility with the provider, but the contract must define replacement duties, system performance, data access, billing corrections, maintenance response, and termination rights. A lower upfront cost is not a good deal if the owner loses control when service quality declines.

Ontario's recent consumer-protection changes also affect the commercial model. The August 2025 OEB amendments make winter disconnection policies, twice-yearly notices, and updated Conditions of Service part of resident-facing operations. Price the staffing, communications, notices, and compliance monitoring required to deliver those duties.

For owners comparing responsibilities, billing administration, and portfolio operations, Axis Meter's property owner services offer one example of structuring metering, billing, maintenance, and reporting as a managed service.

Before a board vote, request a building-specific commercial model, load map, compliance checklist, sample invoice, resident communications plan, commissioning package, and complete service agreement. Require the provider to identify responsibilities before installation, during billing, and when a resident or owner disputes an invoice.

Conclusion

Total meter services work when the owner buys an accountable operating model, not just a box of meters. The provider should connect equipment selection, installation, commissioning, billing, collections, maintenance, resident support, data reporting, and compliance into one documented service.

The 20-year provider-owned model deserves serious consideration because it can preserve owner capital and shift long-term equipment responsibility to the provider. Don't accept that convenience without negotiating service levels, data access, replacement duties, billing correction procedures, regulatory updates, and termination terms.

Ontario owners also need to treat consumer protection as an active operating requirement. The August 2025 OEB amendments make winter disconnection policies, twice-yearly notices, and updated Conditions of Service part of the resident-facing workflow, not merely legal language.

Before approving a project, request a building-specific commercial model, a load map, a compliance checklist, a sample invoice, a resident communications plan, a commissioning package, and a complete service agreement. Choose the provider that can explain who does what before installation, during billing, and when something goes wrong.

Decision standard: If the proposal can't explain the data, the billing, the maintenance, and the resident remedy process, it isn't turnkey enough.
